en: Now, therefore, I shall explain the secret [teaching] in brief and not at length:
the union with Śrī Heruka, which accomplishes all desires and aims,
the *Dākinīcakrasaṃvara*, which is higher even than the highest.
Always abiding in the supreme, most delightful secret, the self of all, consisting of all female messengers, this being Vajrasattva is the supreme bliss;
he is the self-arisen Blessed One, the *Saṃvara* of the *Dākinījāla*.
Emerging in the form of sound, she is the sphere of the conduct of the *samaya*;
difficult to find in the three worlds, she abides in the beginning, middle, and end,
joined with the union of the churner and the act of churning, and with the recitation of mantras and other such practices.
Listen to the yoga and the knowledge of the ritual as proclaimed in the Tantra:
one should constantly worship the Kulikā with the middle and supreme breaths together with scented water, and the Dūtīs at specific times.
The female messengers are innate and accomplished, categorized as inferior, superior, or middling;
with an internal mind, one should cultivate the accomplishment of desire and worship the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with the drops of one's own semen.

By seeing and touching it, and by hearing and remembering it, one is liberated from all sins; of this there is no doubt. This state of being a yogi is supremely meritorious, purifying, and destructive of evil.
Success is achieved through the recitation of mantras, meditation, and ease;
the practitioner, being well-composed, should always observe the commitments (*samaya*). However, by violating the commitments, the desired success is not attained.

Oṃ, homage to Śrī Cakrasaṃvara! By whom the wielder of the Pināka bow was trampled with his left and right feet, by whom the gods, the spirits, and the lords of the asuras were terrified along with the hosts of planets by his wrathful gaze;

he who wears a tiger skin, an elephant hide, a snake, a garland of skulls, and a forest of weapons—to him having bowed, this commentary on that tantra, seeking out the clear vajra-words, is being written by me, Śrī Vajrapāṇi, at the command of Vīreśa.
For the sake of yogins attaining merit and for the attainment of the fruit of Mahāmudrā,
the essence has now been extracted from the *Lakṣābhidhāna-tantra*:
the Śrī Heruka Mahāyoga, the Saṃvara of the Circle of Ḍākinīs.
In this age of the five degenerations, at the request of Vārāhī, the Vajra-holder (Vajradhara) shall reveal this concise tantra for the sake of attaining the fruits of merit and wisdom,
and for the benefit of practitioners who possess short lifespans and little vigor.

By that very means, for those possessed of passion, hatred, and so forth, he— Vajrasattva, the being who consists of all female messengers (*dūtī*), who is great bliss, and who always abides as the secret of the *ḍākinīs*, the secret of the self, and the universal self— is ever-present.
This Blessed One is the Self-Existent, the accomplisher of all desires and aims;
having emerged from the form of sound, he is the sphere of the conduct of the samaya,
difficult to find in the three worlds, and abides at the beginning, middle, and end.
The sequence of the ritual application of mantra, produced from the friction of the churner and the object to be churned,
is the means of expression; that very thing is called the "expressed," by which Heruka—
innate bliss, the supreme middle breath— is made manifest.
Accompanied by the four channels of feces, urine, moon, and sun,
Kulikā Vajravārāhī is the supportless Mahāmudrā;
therefore, the yogin, having abandoned the pleasure of the *karmamudrā*, should worship her.
Thus, this meaning of the consecration, which was not revealed due to the brevity of the tantra and was stated merely as a summary, is here expanded upon by means of a commentary.

In this regard, first of all, having thoroughly considered the subject matter (*abhidheya*), the expression (*abhidhāna*), the relationship (*sambandha*), the purpose (*prayojana*), and the purpose of the purpose (*yojanaprayojana*), the Blessed Lord Śrī Heruka—who bestows the state of Buddhahood in this very life upon those disciples who are free from constraints and act according to their own mental inclinations; who dwells in the supreme secret; who is surrounded by heroes and heroines; and who was requested by Vajravārāhī—taught this Tantra, which is the essence of essences extracted from the *Mūlatantra* known as the *Lakṣābhidhāna*, consisting of seven hundred verses. Herein, the Blessed Lord Heruka, whose nature is wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*), is the subject matter.

The *Tantrarāja* is the title that expresses this [subject matter]; the relationship between these two—the expressed and the expression—is characterized by their mutual status as the signified and the signifier;
and the purpose is the accomplishment of mundane siddhis through the performance of the welfare of sentient beings by means of entering mandalas and so forth.

The attainment of Buddhahood through the practice of Mahāmudrā-siddhi by means of the accumulations of merit and wisdom is the ultimate purpose; having clearly perceived these [points], [the teaching is intended] for those people to be trained who are "devoid of restraint" (*niyamarahitānām*). Here, "restraint" (*niyama*) refers to the vows of a Śrāvaka bhikṣu;
those devoid of such are "devoid of restraint."

Their own mental intention consists of passion, hatred, and so forth; by means of that very mental intention, even in this present life, it bestows Buddhahood through that same method of cultivation for practitioners who, during the age of the five corruptions, possess short lifespans and little vigor— by means of the supreme secret.
The secret is the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), which is the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*); situated therein, abiding in the supreme secret,
and surrounded by heroes and heroines— where "heroes" refers to the twenty-four [deities] such as Khaṇḍakapālin and others who move upon the moon.
The Vīreśvarīs, such as Ḍākinī and the others, have the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) as their intrinsic nature;

he is surrounded by them, thus "surrounded by heroes and heroines. Being requested by Vajravārāhī, the Blessed One Śrī Heruka spoke; for from the syllable *Śrī* comes non-dual gnosis (*jñāna*), and from the syllable *He* comes that which is free from causes.

From the letter *ru* he is free from form (*rūpa*), and from the letter *ka* he is devoid of action (*karana*). Endowed with the qualities of sovereignty and so forth, he possesses *bhaga*; because he shatters the Māras, he is called the Blessed One (*Bhagavān*), the Lord of the Three Realms.
Thus, by that Blessed Śrī Heruka, the essence— a tantra measuring seven hundred verses— was taught from the *Lakṣābhidhāna*, the Root Tantra;
and that Blessed One abides in this very nature of the tantra.
First, he abides by way of the nature of the place of dwelling;
then, he abides by way of the nature of the conduct of the samaya;
then, he abides by way of the nature of the requester and the instructor.
He abides by way of the intrinsic nature of the worship of the *kulikā*; then he abides by way of the intrinsic nature of the worship for the accomplishment of the *dūtī*s;
he abides by way of the intrinsic nature of the meditation on the accomplishment of Rāma.
Then, by means of the drops of bodhicitta, one abides as having the nature of worshiping the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth;
one abides as having the nature of liberation from all evil;
and then one abides as having the nature of accomplishing the state of a yogin.
He abides by way of having the nature of observing the commitments;
thereafter, he abides by way of having the nature of guarding against the breach of commitments;
and he abides by way of having the nature of consuming the five nectars.

Then, in the *gaṇacakra*, by means of the thumb and ring finger, he abides in the nature of tasting the drinking of the *soma*; he abides in the nature of the union of the two organs; and then he abides in the nature of praising divine bliss. Thus, it is said that "divine human bliss does not equal even a sixteenth part of the bliss of the divine immutable"—in this way, the Blessed One is established in the first section on the meaning of the *piṇḍa*.
Then, he abides by way of the nature of fixed locations such as mountain caves;

he abides by way of the nature of the ten principles (*tattva*) beginning with the maṇḍala; then he abides by way of the nature of the worship of the circle of the gurus, heroes, and heroines (*vīreśvarī*);
and he abides by way of the nature of the disciple’s entry into the maṇḍala.

Then, the Blessed One abides in the nature of the bestowal of empowerment; he abides in the nature of the worship of the mudrā-ācārya—thus the Blessed One abides in the section on the mandala-consecration;
then he abides in the nature of the manifestation of the realm of the ḍākinīs.
He abides as the very nature of the extraction of mantras;
he abides as the very nature of the expansion of the activities of the King of Vidyās;
he abides as the very nature of the means for accomplishing the eight mundane siddhis.
Then, he abides as the non-existence of the object of the secret sign (chomā); he abides as the essential nature characterized by the action-seal (karmamudrā);
and then, he abides as the essential nature of the activities of conversing with, approaching, and departing from them.
He abides by way of the intrinsic nature of the characteristics of the ḍākinīs;

he abides by way of the intrinsic nature of the manifestation of seals (mudrā) and counter-seals (pratimudrā); he abides by way of the intrinsic nature of the discourse on the names of the commitments (samaya).
Abiding as the nature of the eight great samayas, both mundane and supramundane,
he then abides as the nature of the consumption of the single *caruka* offering,
and he abides as the nature of the presentation of the *bali* offering.
Then, he abides as the intrinsic nature of the extraction of the mantra of King Sumbha;
he abides as the intrinsic nature of the accomplishment of its range of activities;
and he abides as the intrinsic nature of the meditation on the mantra-image.
Then, he abides by way of having the nature of the cultivation of the reality free from conceptual construction; he abides by way of having the nature of supramundane fire-offerings (*homa*);

then, he abides by way of having the nature of the recitation of mantras such as *Cittavajra*, situated within and at the end of the names of the Heroes (*vīra*) and Heroines (*vīreśvarī*) together with the mantra-words beginning with the four faces; he abides by way of having the nature of the instruction on the twenty-four sites and the ten stages (*bhūmi*) beginning with the sacred seats (*pīṭha*); and he abides by way of having the nature of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) beginning with the head.
He abides as having the nature of the purity of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening;

thereafter, he abides as having the nature of the purity of the twenty-four elements, such as the skull-cup and so forth; and he abides as having the nature of the transformation of the forms of the goddesses, the terrestrial and celestial beings.
He abides as the nature of the mastery over enjoyment and dissolution through the movement of the worship-circle (*pūjācakra*) of the women of the thirty-seven families;
he abides as the nature of the turning of the wheel of Dharma;
he abides as the nature of the Emanation, Enjoyment, and Pure Dharma bodies; and he abides as the nature of the indivisibility of emptiness and compassion.
Thus, the Blessed One Śrī Heruka abides by way of the intrinsic nature of the tantra.

By this very designation, he reveals himself as the subject to be expressed by Vajravārāhī. Now, one might ask: since in every royal tantra the instruction regarding the place of residence begins with "Thus have I heard" and so forth, how is it that in this tantra the Blessed One has stated the instruction regarding the place of residence with "Now, therefore, I shall speak of the secret in brief, not in detail," and so on?
In the *Samājamañjuvajra* and other Yoga and Yoginī Tantras, the words of the Blessed One begin with "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) and so forth;

because of this, some who rely on the literal letter (*vyañjana*) will harbor the opinion that this tantra was not taught by the Blessed One, and thus its status as the word of the Buddha (*bhagavadvacana*) is not established.

Therefore, it is said here that whatever must be stated regarding the future time by foolish people who rely on the literal letter (*vyañjana*), such as "Thus have I heard" and so forth— without [the introduction] to the *Tantrarāja*— has not been spoken by the Blessed One.
That is not [the case].
Why is it that the Blessed One has taught the four reliances elsewhere, as follows?
Relying on the meaning, not relying on the letter; relying on gnosis, not relying on consciousness;
relying on the definitive meaning, not relying on the interpretable meaning; relying on the Dharma, not relying on the person.

Therefore, according to the words of the Blessed One, reliance upon the letter (*vyañjanapratisaraṇatā*) has nowhere been taught by the Blessed One in any vehicle. The collection of vowels and consonants is merely a designation (*saṃjñāmātra*) that indicates the existence or non-existence of things (*bhāva-abhāva-dharma*) for those who possess designations.

In this regard, multiple designations can occur for even a single thing characterized by existence or non-existence, yet among them no single designation will be either primary or secondary, because all of them indicate the same single state of existence or non-existence—just as the terms "woman," "lady," "young woman," and so forth, all indicate the same state of possessing breasts, hair, and the like.

Likewise, because [terms such as] "sky-flower," "space-ness," and "tastelessness" establish the nature of non-existence, the relationship between the designation (*saṃjñā*) and the designated (*saṃjñin*) is to be understood by yogis in this way throughout all cases. Here, the vowel *a* (the letter *a*), which establishes emptiness, becomes the dative case ending *-e*; therefore, by the designation *e*, the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*)—the support of all—is grasped.

Likewise, in the *Dākinīvajrapañjara*, the Blessed One said: "In the sky, which is unborn, pure, and luminous where there is no space, in the universal abode of vajras, the delightful dwelling in the all-pervading element"—and so forth, up to the end of the passage: "He always dwells in the supreme, most delightful secret, the self of all. Thus, under the guise of various specific designations, the term for his "dwelling" (*vijahāra*) has been explained.

Similarly, in the *Śrīsamāja* and other tantras, it is said: "Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One dwelt in the wombs (*bhaga*) of the Vajra Ladies, who are the heart of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas."
This [foundation] also has many names:
it is considered to be Bhaga, the Lotus, the Pure, the Abode of Bliss, Sukhāvatī, the Unsupported Lion Throne, Suchness (tathatā), and the Perfection (pāramitā). Thus is the foundation.
Likewise,

the object of meditation (ādheya) is celebrated by many names such as "the wielder of the thunderbolt," "the giver of boons," "the speaker," "innate bliss," "the imperishable," "the auspicious," "the peaceful," "the benevolent," "the Lord," "the all-pervading," and "the supreme."
In the *Nāmasamgīti*, the Blessed One has revealed that the Gnosis Body (*jñānakāya*) is without parts (*niranvaya*);

thus, the support (*dhāra*) is the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), while the supported (*ādheya*) is omniformity (*sarvākāratva*) which is non-conceptual and compassion (*karuṇā*) which is without objective support (*nirālambā*). Therefore, it is said in another Tantra: "That divine form shaped like the letter *E*, adorned in its center with the syllable *Vaṃ*, is the abode (*ālaya*) of all blisses, a jewel-casket of the Buddhas. Likewise: "Without beginning or end, peaceful, the exhaustion of existence and non-existence, the all-pervading Lord (*vibhu*)."

"Bodhicitta is known as the indivisibility of emptiness and compassion. Thus, in many various tantras, this yoga consisting of wisdom and means was taught by the Blessed One. Therefore, Buddhists should not say: "That tantra was taught by the Blessed One in which [the formula] *evam mayā* and so forth exists;

that in which it does not exist is not [a teaching of his]. In this Mantra system, grasping at faults regarding the unseen Dharma constitutes a root downfall (*mūlāpatti*). From a root downfall, one goes to the Avīci hell—this is for those who are conceited due to their false learning.

Thus, for this reason, the teaching of the tantra in this [text] beginning with "Now, the secret" is not contradictory, because it establishes the Dharma consisting of wisdom and means, whose nature is emptiness and compassion.

Regarding this, it is said in the *Lakṣābhidhāna*: "That tantra in which the identity of emptiness and compassion is revealed, and which is the means of accomplishment for the Lord of the World—that tantra was taught by the Buddha. This refers to the attainment of worldly accomplishments through the conventional truth of the world.

"The cultivation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-bhāvanā*) and likewise the ritual procedure for the recitation of mantras have been taught [by the Tathāgatas] for the sake of accomplishing the Gnosis-Body (*jñānakāya*). However, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), cultivation free from all conceptualization has been taught. Thus ends the rule for the consecration (*pratisthāpana*) according to the Tantra. Now, the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) and the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) stated in the Tantra are being elaborated, beginning with the words:
"Next, I shall explain the secret... and so forth.

Now, immediately after the *vajrabhairava-samādhi*, the Blessed Lord Heruka, having entered the *samādhi* of the *samvara* of the *cakravartin* of dākinīs, addressed Vajravārāhī from the *Lakṣābhidhāna*: "O Vajravārāhī, listen! I shall speak to you in brief, and not at length, that very secret called Heruka which is proclaimed in the *tantra* known as the *Lakṣābhidhāna*—the yoga and the knowledge of the ritual procedure. [Vajravārāhī asked: "For what reason, O Blessed One, do you teach a short *tantra* instead of the root *tantra*?
The Blessed One replied:
In this age of the five degenerations, the humans of Jambudvīpa— especially those in the land of the Āryas— will have short lifespans and little wisdom;
those who are Vajrācāryas will fall into root downfalls,
and the monks will become practitioners of the ten unwholesome actions.
Householders will become consumers of the wealth of the Three Jewels;
scholars will become commentators on tantras they have not heard;
and out of pride in their own scholarship, they will compose word-by-word glosses and commentaries on the tantras.

Having taught the meaning of the tantras in a perverted manner, those foolish Buddhists will go to hell; out of the blindness of their faith, they will perform services for householders who act as teachers,
and they will revile those who bear the banner of the Omniscient One.
Those who are disciples will become seekers of faults in the true guru;
they will offer praise and worship to false gurus who are like devouring non-dualists, and they will not act according to the word of the Buddha as taught for the propitiation of the guru.
They will be teachers of the Dharma who promote the ten unwholesome actions;
they will be practitioners attached to external food, drink, and enjoyments;
and women will become excessively greedy for sensual pleasures.

Therefore, the teaching of the *alpatantra* (short tantra) from the *sarvamūlatantra* (all-root tantra) by the Buddha must be understood by wise seekers of liberation through the instructions of a true guru, as expressed in other tantras, and through commentaries composed by Bodhisattvas.
For this reason, I shall speak of the secret in brief rather than in detail;
"the secret, the secret" is taught in the sense of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) as the *karmamudrā*, which is the *bhaga*.
In the definitive sense, the perfection of wisdom is emptiness;
"union with Śrī Heruka" means that "Śrī" is innate bliss (sahajānanda).
*He* means devoid of the causes of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) and the knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*);
*ru* means free from the characteristics of form; *ka* means devoid of the instruments such as the eye; it is characterized by non-referential compassion, and its union with emptiness is oneness.

"I shall explain the non-duality of emptiness and compassion"—this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*). Śrī Heruka is the male organ; his union with the female vulva is their oneness. "I shall explain" [this] for the sake of the accumulation of merit for those foolish people who desire the bliss of the two organs, and for the sake of liberating the mind from other objects.
"The accomplisher of all desired aims" is a qualification of the ritual action (*karmapada*).
"I shall speak"—it should be understood that the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used everywhere in this sense of the agent.

Here, according to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), the "object of all desires" refers to the mundane sovereignty of qualities such as *aṇimā* and so forth, which arises through the yoga of the mantra, action, knowledge, and seal (*mudrā*);

its "accomplisher" is the previously mentioned "knowledge of wisdom" (*prajñājñāna*). According to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), "all desires" refers to Vajrasattva, the Perfectly Awakened One; his "object" is the turning of the wheel of Dharma, consisting of omniscience, the ten powers, the four forms of fearlessness, and so forth.
I shall explain the yoga that accomplishes it— the yoga that accomplishes all desired aims and is inseparable from emptiness and compassion—
as "even higher than the highest."

In this context, "superior" means that the bliss of the human realm, which pertains to the objects of desire, is inferior; superior to that is the bliss of the perfected beings belonging to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, which is endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers and so forth.

Furthermore, compared even to that superior [bliss], the bliss of the Omniscient One is the supreme excellence—endowed with all qualities of sovereignty, the teacher of all phenomena, possessing all aspects, and all-pervading;
thus it is "superior even to the superior."
Regarding the phrase "the *Cakrasaṃvara* of the *ḍākinīs*":
here, according to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), the *ḍākinīs* are Vajraḍākinī and the others;
internally, they are the thirty-six channels (*nāḍīs*) situated at the gates of the mouth and so forth within the wheels of gnosis, mind, speech, and body.

These very [sites] are designated by the names "Self-Pīṭha" and so forth; from Ucchiṣṭa up to Śmaśāna, they are located in the eight directions outside of Meru according to the sequence to be described. One should understand that this is the instruction regarding the locations, such as the countries and the heads, for those who possess the nature of being both the support and the supported.
This is the *cakra*, the assembly, of these ḍākinīs.

Its "convention" (*saṃvara*) is its unity, the gathering together with Heruka in the self-mandala (*ātmapīṭha*) and so forth, known as the Saṃvara of the circle of ḍākinīs. Thus, Heruka, together with the heroes (*vīra*), consists of twenty-five aspects;
Vajravārāhī, together with the mistresses of heroes (*vīreśvarī*), consists of thirty-seven aspects.
Regarding the phrase "the *samvara*, the assembly (*melāpaka*) of these ḍākinīs, together with Heruka and the twenty-four heroes":
here, the *samvara* refers to the union of the twelve messengers with Heruka,
and the *samvara* of the twenty-four messengers with the heroes.

That very [reality] is expressed here by means of the union of vowels and consonants (*ālikāli*) through the seed-syllables of mantra. In this regard, there are thirty-six *Yoginī* tantras; with each single syllable beginning with the letter *ka*, accompanied by the collection of vowels, they consist of thirty-six mandala deities.
Without a leader (*nāyaka*), the two leaders [of the male and female] consist of thirty-seven [deities].
Herein, first, the *Kavajra-tantra* is described.
In the activity of the wheel of the knowledge of the womb, the syllable *hūṃ* consists of the five voids; on the petals of the cardinal directions are *A*, *Ā*, *AM*, *AH*;
and on the petals of the intermediate directions are *KA*, *KĀ*, *KAM*, *KAH*.

By means of the distinction of the *guṇa* vowels, in the cardinal directions of the cremation ground are *ka kā kaṃ kaḥ*; in the corners are *kā krū klaṃ*. Thus, in the *cittacakra*, in the cardinal directions are *ki kri ku klṛ*, and in the intermediate directions are *kī krī kū klū*. By means of the distinction of *vṛddhi* vowels, in the cardinal directions of the *vākcakra* are *ke kar ko kal*, and in the intermediate directions are *kai kār kau kāl*.

In the wheel of action (*karmacakra*), by means of the substitution of *yaṇ*, there arise *KYA KRA KVA KLA* in the cardinal directions and *KYĀ KRĀ KVĀ KLĀ* in the intermediate directions; thus, the consonants produced by the qualities of wind, fire, water, and earth consist of twenty-four elements in the three wheels. Together with those produced by the quality of the void-vowels in the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*)—specifically those produced in the eight cremation grounds—it becomes twelvefold.
Therefore, the *saṃvara* of those *ḍākinīs* whose nature is the sound of emptiness, together with the embodiment of non-referential compassion—

the Lord who possesses twelve eyes— in union (*dvandva*) with Vajravārāhī; and the union of the twenty-four Heroines with the twenty-four Heroes— this is the *Ḍākinīcakrasaṃvara* according to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).

Thus, beginning with the Vajra of the letter Kha, they are as follows: KA KHA GA GHA NA; CA CHA JA JHA ÑA; TA THA DA DHA NA; PA PHA BA BHA MA; TA THA DA DHA NA; SA PA ȘA ŚA KA; LA VA RA YA; HA KṢA—these are the thirty-six leaders of the Yoginī Tantras.
Even the leaders of the Yoga Tantras,

when produced from a single seed-syllable, become members of the mandala; however, those members of the mandala who are generated from thirty-six distinct seed-syllables belong to distinct tantric families.

"They are not to be understood as belonging to a single family; rather, the three families, the five families, the single nature, and the hundred families [are to be known]," according to the word of the Blessed One.

Thus, the Tathāgata’s rule is that the *tantra*, which consists of various families, must be understood by the yogin by relying on the reliance upon the meaning (*arthapratisaraṇatā*). Conventionally (*lokasaṃvṛtyā*), the *Ḍākinīcakrasaṃvara* is for the sake of accomplishing worldly attainments (*laukikasiddhi*). In its definitive sense (*nītārtha*), the *Ḍākinīcakrasaṃvara* refers to the *ḍākinīs*, who are the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣikadharma*).
Their *cakra* is a collection characterized by the *dharmakāya*, whose nature is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Its "vow" (*saṃvara*)—that is, its oneness—with the *svābhāvikakāya*, which consists of non-referential compassion, is as follows: here, compassion is the moon, the bodhicitta characterized by the twenty-five lunar digits, the unobstructed great bliss;
and the sun is the twelvefold nature of emptiness.
The *saṃvara* together with that is the *Ḍākinīcakrasaṃvara*; "I shall explain it"—this is the rule of action (*kriyāniyama*).

Thus, in the sequence described: "Abiding always within the secret, supreme, and delightful, the very self of all, consisting of all female messengers (*dūtī*), the being (*sattva*) Vajrasattva is supreme bliss. So it is said.

Here, in this aforementioned void-element (śūnyadhātu), which possesses all self-natures and exists at all times—past, future, and present—one abides as a being consisting entirely of messengers (dūtīmaya) because of the absence of the phenomena of arising and destruction.
These messengers are the *ḍākinīs*; they are equal to space, have abandoned the obscurations of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, and move through space.
From the *dhātupāṭha*, [the root] *vaihāyasa-gamana* (flying through the air) is established;

therefore, the village deities (*grāmadaivatyāḥ*) who cause harm to all sentient beings and reside in the *pīṭhas*, *upapīṭhas*, and so forth, are in their true nature purified as the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*). A being consisting of these is "consisting of all female messengers" (*sarvadūtīmaya*), which is the *dharmakāya* characterized by the three realms. [8a]
"Vajrasattva is supreme bliss" means that the fourth body, the sahajakāya, is supreme bliss, which is to say immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*);
the unity of these two, the dharmakāya and the sahajakāya, is called Vajrasattva.
"Vajra" refers to the Dharmakāya, which is emptiness and wisdom;
"Sattva" refers to the Sahajakāya, which is compassion and skillful means.
Thus, Heruka, whose nature consists of wisdom and skillful means, is designated as Vajrasattva through their union.

"This Blessed One, the Self-Arisen, is the *Dākinījālasaṃvara*. Here, "Self-Arisen" refers to Brahmā; and he is Vairocana, the Body-Vajra, because it is stated in another tantra that "Brahmā is the Holder of the Body-Vajra. This should be understood through other tantras as follows; for instance, the Blessed One said in the *Māyājāla*: "The Self-Arisen born from space, the great fire of the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*)."

"Vairocana is the great radiance; Vairocana is the light of gnosis," and so forth—this should be understood through the verses ending with "the vajra-hook, the great noose. The self-arisen Vairocana is the *nirmāṇakāya*, endowed with the excellence of all aspects; such is the rule of the *Dākinījālasaṃvara*.
Having emerged in the form of sound, she is the sphere of the conduct of the *samaya*.

Thus, through the single yoga of the Sahaja, Dharma, and Nirmāṇa bodies, the Saṃbhoga body consists of sound (*nāda*), characterized by the unstruck resonance (*anāhata-dhvani*) of all gnoses. Its essential nature is the form of mantra, accessible through the practices of the *samaya*. The mantra-deity in the form of sound is the unstruck speech;
this practice of the *samaya* will be explained below, by which it becomes accessible—that is, attainable.
And thus the Blessed One said: "The Dharma-drum, the great sound; the Dharma-bell, the great resonance; the drum of the Dharma in the ten directions, which is the non-abiding nirvana."

"Difficult to find in the three worlds, abiding as the beginning, middle, and end"— this knowledge, consisting of the innate, enjoyment, and emanation bodies, unified as a single essence of gnosis, mind, speech, and body, abides in the three worlds of heaven, earth, and the underworld; it is difficult for those of little merit to encounter among all phenomena.

"Beginning, middle, and end" means established in the past, future, and present times; thus it is "established in beginning, middle, and end. "Endowed with the union of the churner and the churning, along with mantra-recitation and so forth" means that here, for yogins, that very gnosis arises through the union of the churner and the churning—that is, through the union of the two organs—and likewise through the previously mentioned yoga and the knowledge of the ritual, as well as the worldly knowledge accomplished by means of the ritual, mantra-recitation, and meditation on the maṇḍala-circle.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is indicated that [the goal] is accomplished through mantras, fire-offerings (*homādi*), and other means.
That very knowledge is "knowledge of the ritual" (*vidhijñāna*) and "worldly knowledge.

Thus, listen now to this tantra, which is the essence of essences, being taught by me here in the *Vajravārāhī* [tantra], though it was previously described in the extensive *Lakṣābhidhāna*—namely, the yoga mentioned before, consisting of emptiness and compassion, and, by the word "and," the knowledge of the ritual as well, which was proclaimed in the tantra.

The relationship between the teacher and the requester, together with the relationship between the subject matter and the expression, has been elucidated by the commentary according to the definitive and interpretable meanings of the Blessed One’s teaching.
Now, the worship of the *Kulikā* is described by the passage beginning with "by the middle and supreme breath," and so forth.
Here, the *madhyamā* is the *avadhūtī*, the channel flowing as a line of fire between *Ālikāli*.

Among its breaths—numbering twenty-one thousand six hundred and sixty per day and night—there are six hundred and seventy-five breaths during the twelve zodiacal transits (*saṃkrānti*) within a single day and night.

The remaining twenty-one hundred and ninety (21,090) breaths flow through the *lalanā* and *rasanā* channels during those twelve zodiacal signs (*lagna*). Specifically, in each odd sign beginning with Aries, eighteen hundred breaths flow through the *lalanā*;
likewise, in each even sign beginning with Taurus, [eighteen hundred] flow through the *rasanā*.

At the time of each transition (*saṃkrānti*), the breaths at the beginning and end of those two [channels]—namely fifty-six and a quarter (56¼)—belong to the central *avadhūtī* between the even and odd signs.

The lowest [breaths] among living beings are those that bring about death; they arise from the *kulika* at the time of death, have the nature of flux (*kṣara*), and cause untimely death and demise because they flow as the fire of time (*kālāgni*). The remaining breaths—five hundred and fifty-six less one-quarter—are the eighteen hundred breaths that flow through the five mandalas of *lalanā*, *rasanā*, and *avadhūtī*.
Within these, the breaths flowing through each individual mandala number three hundred and sixty, less eleven and one-quarter breaths.
Here, the five mandalas beginning with space belong to the lalanā;
the five beginning with earth belong to the rasanā on the left and right respectively.
In this case, on the petals of the navel lotus, there are—in order from the center, east, south, north, and west—the mandalas of space, wind, fire, water, and earth.
In the pericarp is the sixth, the equinox, the mandala of gnosis (*jñāna*).
Above the two nostrils, as in the center, above, on the right, and on the left, and below, respectively: on the left are space and the others; on the right are earth and the others.

The sixth consists of fifty-six breaths and a quarter occurring simultaneously through both nostrils. These breaths, which flow through the left and right channels of these mandalas, having been introduced into the central *avadhūtī* channel either by the power of the movement of the *nāḍīs* or by the power of *prāṇāyāma*, become common [to all] and serve as deceivers of untimely death (*ariṣṭamaraṇa*), because they have been made to flow within the central channel through the power of yoga.

In this context, these are supreme, born from the great vital breath (*mahāprāṇa*), destroyers of the common inferior [states], bestowers of the bliss of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣarasukha*), personally realized through the knowledge of yogis, devoid of the nature of the unchanging bliss of the objects of the external senses, accessible to the divine senses, numbering the cycles of breaths (*śvāsacakra*), having the form of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), and because they do not fall from great bliss (*mahāsukha*). Among them, each individual breath of supreme unchanging bliss is the "supreme" and the "middle-superior" breath; therefore, it is said: "by that middle-superior breath together with scented water."
Here, "scent" refers to the *lalanā*, which flows with the wind of Vairocana and the moon, both below and above;
"water" refers to the *rasanā*, which flows with the wind of Mitra and the sun, both below and above;
and the "middle" refers to the *avadhūtī*, which flows with the winds of semen, menstrual blood, Rāhu, and the fire of time (*kālāgni*), both below and above.

In this central *avadhūtī*, the inferior exhaling breath (*kṣara-śvāsa*) brings death to living beings; the middling [exhaling breath] is common, which deceives [the signs of] untimely death (*ariṣṭa-maraṇa*); the superior is the bliss of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara-sukha*), which bestows the siddhi of Mahāmudrā. Therefore, it is called the "middling-superior breath. That very [breath], when joined below and above with the channels of feces, urine, moon, sun, semen, blood, Rāhu, and Kālāgni, becomes of one flavor (*samarasībhūta*) with the *nādī*; it holds the four drops of bodhicitta, is the union of body, speech, and mind, has its semen drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*), and is the single-pronged vajra.

By that middle and supreme breath, accompanied by scented water, having the nature of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), free from subject and object, the great breath of the Vajra-holder, devoid of the causes of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) and knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*), arisen from the cause of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), personally realized through the wisdom of the yogin, with the objects and sense faculties unified as one; by means of the *caṇḍālī* ignited at the navel, the nectar melted from the moon at the forehead—once the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases have been consumed—and flowing upwards without falling; by the body of innate joy (*sahajakāya*) produced from the supreme syllable, free from the sounds *ali*, *kali*, *hūṃ*, and *phaṭ*; free from the cultivation of the maṇḍala circle; transcending the external phenomena of mantra-recitation, mudrā-consecration, and the transmission of the Guru’s command; non-abiding in both cyclic existence (*bhava*) and nirvāṇa; inseparable from compassion and emptiness; in the form of the drops of bodhicitta flowing uninterruptedly from the forehead to the vajra-jewel; by that middle and supreme breath of great, non-falling passion.
"By this, one should constantly worship the Kulikā.

Here, the Kulikā is the central Avadhūtī, Vajravārāhī, free from obscurations, devoid of subject and object, the destroyer of the hosts of Māras for yogins, the destroyer of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases as well as the bodhicitta for the ignorant; she who is endowed with the non-falling of bodhicitta, the Perfection of Wisdom, Emptiness, and Suchness—this Kulikā is called the Lotus.

With that *kulikā*—by means of the method consisting of the supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*), the non-falling drop of bodhicitta, the moon-like fluid of great passion (*mahārāga*), the supreme central breath, and the scented water produced from the *kulikā*—one should worship that very same one’s own *prajñā*.
This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*): the yogin should effect the unity of the apprehended and the apprehender, of the object of knowledge and knowledge, and of emptiness and compassion.

"One should worship constantly" means at all times—whether impure or pure, standing or seated, sleeping or engaged in the activities of body, speech, and mind—one who is devoted to the supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*), free from longing for the enjoyment of all sensual desires, and who, through divine senses, is not attached to the enjoyment of objects seen externally; thus, by means of the intermediate and superior breaths, the procedure for the worship of the *Kulikā* was taught by the Blessed One for the sake of attaining the *Mahāmudrā-siddhi* according to the supramundane truth (*lokottarasatya*).

Now, for the sake of accomplishing worldly siddhis, the procedure for the worship of the dūtīs through the five offerings and other rites—using the pill of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta-gulikā*) at the gathering (*melāpaka*) where the dūtīs move—is described both externally and internally according to specific times, beginning with the words "here, time is first of two kinds," and so forth. Here, time is indeed twofold: external and internal;
[it is] year by year and day by day, respectively.

Its specific detail is the distinction of time (*kālaviśeṣa*): externally, it is the zodiacal wheel consisting of twelve ascendants; this is the distinction of time. Here, externally, the distinction of time for each year consists of days, fortnights, months, seasons, *yugas*, ages, and solstices; whereas internally, the distinction of time for each day consists of breaths, *pānīyapala*s, *ghaṭikā*s, *muhūrta*s, half-watch periods, ascendants, watches, twilights, and the full day-and-night (*ahorātra*). This is the distinction of time.

Externally, the specific divisions of time in each year consist of thirty-sixty days (360), twenty-four fortnights, twelve months, six seasons, four *yugas* consisting of three months each, three periods consisting of four months each, and two solstices (*ayana*) consisting of six months each. The aggregate of these is one year, which is "time" (*kāla*). Internally, this same time is present every day.

Twenty-one thousand six hundred inhalations and exhalations, three thousand six hundred *pala* of water, sixty *ghatikās*, thirty *muhūrtas*, sixteen half-watches (*ardhaprahara*), twelve zodiacal signs (*lagna*), eight watches (*prahara*), and four twilights (*sandhyā*) constitute a single day; this collection is "time" (*kāla*).

Thus, just as there is a specific division of time externally through the movement of the sun, so too is there a specific division of time internally through the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
By means of that specific division of time, one should worship the female messengers (*dūtī*) every year and every day.
The female messengers (dūtī) are the thirty-six yoginīs beginning with Vajradākinī and ending with Yamamathanī; one should worship them.

In this context, just as the messenger goddesses (*dūtī*) are to be worshipped, so too are the innate ones (*sahaja*) and the accomplished ones (*siddha*). In reverse order, the twenty-four [deities] beginning with Vajrasattva—the inferior, middling, and superior—are the bestowers of the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of the subterranean, terrestrial, and celestial realms within the wheels of body, speech, and mind.
They too are to be worshipped at specific times; such is the rule of the Tathāgatas.

Thus, one should worship the messenger goddesses, the innate ones, and the accomplished ones in the external *gaṇacakra* with the pill of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), with meats such as beef and human flesh, and with the blameless commitments (*samaya*) and the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*).
Within the internal [body], in the wheels of knowledge, mind, speech, and body, there is a specific time determined by the movement of the sun and the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
By means of that specific time, there is the movement of the female messenger (*dūtī*).

Through the movement of the female messengers (*dūtī*), there is the experience (*bhoga*), dissolution (*laya*), and authority (*adhikāra*) of the Kulikā, as well as the sovereignty (*prabhutva*). Furthermore, for the thirty-six female messengers,
there is experience in the present time and dissolution and sovereignty in the future time, according to their respective order.
In the past time there is authority;
at sunrise there is enjoyment; at midday there is authority.
The principle is that mastery resides at the point of sunset and dissolution occurs at midnight;
thus, externally on the day of enjoyment (*bhogadina*), and internally during the time of enjoyment (*bhogavelā*), there is the movement of the Yoginīs,
and through the movement of the Yoginīs, there is the gathering of the wheels (*cakramelāpaka*).
"One should worship the *dinabhoginī* and the *velābhoginī* during the *cakramelāpaka*"; thus, there is enjoyment (*bhoga*) in childhood, authority (*adhikāra*) in youth,
and sovereignty (*prabhutva*) in old age.
At the time of death, during the hour of midnight, dissolution occurs;
from that dissolution, there is rebirth, which is called "the fool.

Thus, according to specific times—by way of the division of the four twilights (*catuḥsaṃdhyā*), the division of the eight watches (*prahara*), and the division of the twenty-four fortnights—there is a rule everywhere regarding the authority over enjoyment and dissolution, as well as the lordship, of the thirty-six yoginīs according to their specific times.
Now the ritual of worship is described:

here, whether externally or internally, the practitioner should at all times worship Kulikā Vajravārāhī by means of the supreme central breath characterized by great immutable bliss, for the sake of attaining Mahāmudrā; or, for the sake of worldly accomplishments, he should worship Vajradākinī and the others in their proper order according to specific times.

In this regard, externally, during the transition of the sun into Capricorn (makara-saṃkrānti) and at the rising of the eastern face, one should worship Vajradākinī for the purpose of accomplishing the rite of slaying.

At the transition of the sun into Capricorn (*meṣasaṃkrānti*), when the southern face arises, one should worship Lāmā for the sake of accomplishing the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*); at the transition into Cancer (*karkaṭasaṃkrānti*), when the western face arises, one should worship Kandarohā for the sake of paralyzing (*stambhana*);

and at the transition into Libra (*tulāsaṃkrānti*), when the northern face arises, one should worship Rūpiṇī for the sake of pacification (*śāntika*). Thus, O Mantrin, at the end of the three months following each of these three transitions, there occurs the increase or decrease of the sun’s power, which constitutes the four *yuga*-transitions (*sandhyā*) of the year.

On the days of their respective transits, according to the stated sequence, the four *ḍākinīs*—the *bhoginīs* who are the goddesses of the Lord’s eastern, southern, western, and northern directions—are to be understood through the divisions of the Body, Speech, Mind, and Wisdom. This is the rule that they are for the accomplishment of rites such as *māraṇa* (killing) and so forth, and not by way of the distinction of the elements such as earth and so on.

Thus, in every case where it will be explained hereafter regarding the accomplishment of the expansion of activities (*karmaprasara*) through the division of faces, this is the rule for worship. Now, the worship of the goddesses of the cremation grounds is described:
here, on the day of the transit of Capricorn (*makara*), [one worships] Kākāsyā for the purpose of *uccāṭana* (driving away).
On the day of the half-Kumbha [solar term], one should worship Ulūkāsyā for the purpose of attraction;
on the day of the Meṣa-saṃkrānti, Śvānāsyā for the purpose of killing;
and on the day of the half-Vṛṣabha, Śūkarāsyā for the purpose of nourishment.
On the day of the Cancer transit, the yogi should worship Yamadāhī for the purpose of paralyzing; on the half-day of Leo, Yamadūtī for the purpose of deluding;
on the day of the Libra transit, Yamadamstrinī for the purpose of paralyzing;
and on the half-day of Scorpio, Yamamathanī for the purpose of creating enmity. Thus, there are eight watches (praharas) comprising one and a half months each within the year.
In those initial days, the rule is that the eight Yoginīs, as the enjoyers (bhoginī), [are to be worshipped] according to the stated sequence for a duration of one and a half months each.
Now the worship of the goddesses of the wheels of mind, speech, and body is described.

Here, on the new moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship Pracandā and Kandakapālin for the purpose of accomplishing the rite of slaying; on the full moon day, one should worship Candākṣī and Mahākaṅkāla for the purpose of subjugation.
On the new moon of Puṣya, one should worship Prabhāvatī and Kaṅkāla for the purpose of immobilization;
on the full moon, Mahānāsā and Vikṛtadaṃṣṭrin for the purpose of nourishment; and on the new moon of Māgha, Vīramatī and Surāvairin for the purpose of pacification.

On the full moon day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship Kharvarī and Amitābha for the purpose of deluding; on the new moon day of Phalguna, Laṅkeśvarī and Vajraprabha for the purpose of summoning;
and on the full moon day [of Caitra], Drumacchāyā and Vajradeha for the purpose of creating enmity.

Thus, during the eight days of the fortnights within the four months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, the eight Heroines (Vīreśvarīs) and their consorts (Bhoginīs) reside in the Mind Wheel (Cittacakra) according to the stated sequence.
Now the worship of the wheel of speech (*vākcakra*) is described:
here, on the new moon day of Caitra, one should [offer] Airāvatī and Aṅkurika for the purpose of eradication;
on the full moon day, one should offer Mahābhairavā and *vajra-tila* for the purpose of causing distress.
On the new moon of Vaiśākha, one should worship Vāyuvega and Mahāvīra for the purpose of paralyzing an army;
on the full moon, Surābhakṣī and Vajrahūṃkāra for the purpose of causing rain from the clouds;
on the new moon of Jyeṣṭha, Śyāmadevī and Subhadra for the purpose of pacifying fever; and on the full moon, Subhadrā and Vajrabhadra for the purpose of piercing the underworld (pātāla).
On the new moon of Āṣāḍha, Hayakarṇā is [worshipped] for the sake of possession;
on the full moon, Virūpākṣā is [worshipped] for the sake of shattering the clouds.

Thus, during the eight days of the fortnights of the four months beginning with Caitra, according to the stated sequence, the eight Vīras and Vīreśvarīs, or the Bhoginīs, reside in the Wheel of Speech (vākcakra).
Now the worship of the body wheel (*kāyacakra*) is described:
here, on the new moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should [worship] Cakravegā and Mahābala for the sake of accomplishing the great sword;
on the full moon day, one should [worship] Khaṇḍarohā and Ratnavajra for the sake of subjugating the daughters of the *nāgas*.
On the new moon day of Bhādrapada, one should worship Śauṇḍinī Hayagrīva for the purpose of paralyzing the king of nāgas;

on the full moon day, Cakravarmiṇī Ākāśagarbha for the purpose of accomplishing the great elixir; on the new moon day of Āśvina, Suvīrā Heruka for the purpose of accomplishing the fruit of immortality;
and on the full moon day, Mahābalā Padmanarteśvara for the purpose of accomplishing ritual substances.
On the new moon day of Kārttika, one should worship Cakravartinī Vairocanī for the sake of accomplishing the Jewel;
on the full moon day, one should worship Mahāvīryā Vajrasattvā for the sake of shaking the three worlds.
Thus, during the eight days of the four months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, according to the stated sequence, the Heroines and the powerful Mistresses of Heroes are the consorts in the Body Wheel.
Alternatively, on the day of the Sun's transit into Scorpio during the half-day of Scorpio,
on the day of the transit into Sagittarius during the half-day of Sagittarius,
and on the day of the transit into Capricorn during the half-day of Capricorn.

During the transit into Aquarius (kumbha-saṃkrānti) and during the half-days of Aquarius, the eight Vīras and Vīreśvarīs are the Bhoginīs in the mind-wheel (citta-cakra). Likewise, during the transit into Pisces (mīna-saṃkrānti) and its half,
during the transit into Aries (meṣa-saṃkrānti) and its half, and during the transit into Taurus (vṛṣa-saṃkrānti) and its half.

During the eight days beginning with the day of the mid-point of Gemini and the transition of Gemini, the eight Heroes, Heroines, and Bhoginīs abide in the Vāk-cakra according to the stated order; likewise during the mid-point of Cancer and the transition of Cancer,
and during the mid-point of Leo and the transition of Leo.

During the eight days— namely, during the half of Virgo at the transition into Virgo and the half of Libra at the transition into Libra— the eight Ravi-īśvarīs, who are the Bhoginīs, reside in the Body Wheel (kāyacakra) in their respective order.
In this context, the current first year should be taken according to the three-year divisions beginning with Prabhava;
namely:
Prabhava, Vibhava, Śukla, Pramoda, and Prajāpati.
Aṅgiras, Śrīmukha, Bhāva, Yuvan, and likewise Dhātṛ.
Īśvara, Bahudhanya, Pramādī, Vikrama, Vṛṣa, Citrabhānu, Subhānu, Taraṇa, Pārthiva, and Avyaya.
Sarvajit, Sarvadhārī, Virodhin, Vikṛta, Khara, Nandana, Vijaya, Jaya, Manmatha, and Durmukha.
Hemalamba, Vilambin, Vikarin, Sharvari, Plava, Shubhakrit, Shobhana, Krodhin, Vishvavasu, and Parabhava.
Pravanga, Kīlaka, Saumya, Sādhāraṇa, Virodhakṛt, Paridhāvī, Pramādī, Ānanda, Rākṣasa, and Anala.
Piṅgala, Kāladūtī, Siddhārtha, Raudra, Durmati, Dundubhi, Rudhirodgārī, Raktākṣī, Krodhana, and Kṣaya.
Thus, among the sixty-year cycle,
at the end of every three years, the first triad of years should again be taken according to the distinction of the three qualities (*guṇas*).
In that regard, during the first year, one should recite the mantra of the four-faced one (*caturvaktra*) together with the names of the four goddesses, divided into periods of three months each.

Then, in the second year, one should recite the eight-syllable mantra accompanied by the names of the eight yoginīs, according to the division of each fortnight. Then, in the third year, one should recite the limb-by-limb garland-mantra (pratyanga-mālāmantra) accompanied by the names of the twenty-four goddesses for the very purpose of accomplishing the previously mentioned expansion of activities (*karmaprasara*).

Thus, having accomplished the thirty-six dākinīs through three years, six years, nine years, or twelve years, the mantrin then performs the expansion of all activities, which is the accomplishment of mundane siddhis; such is the rule of the Tathāgata.
Thus, within oneself, there are four junctions (*saṃdhyā*) consisting of eight watches (*prahara*), each comprising two and a half *daṇḍa*s, which constitute twenty-four lunar fortnights of *lagna*s.
During these times, every day, one should worship Vajradākinī and the others for the sake of accomplishing the previously mentioned siddhis.
This is the rule for the procedure of worshipping the female messengers (*dūtī*) according to the specific times.
Now, the specific time mentioned in other tantras is stated:
here, the specific time has been taught by the Blessed One in various tantras.
This has been stated merely by way of indication;
it should be understood here according to the intention expressed in that tantra, for "a tantra is to be understood through another tantra," as per the word of the Tathāgata.
Thus is this particular time.
First, in the four seats (*catuṣpīṭha*), those zodiac signs (*lagna*) beginning with Capricorn (*makara*) are the twelve breaths (*nāḍī*) beginning with Rohiṇī;
those twelve months beginning with Puṣya are the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga*) beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*).
Thus, externally and internally, there are twelve zodiac signs for every year and for every day.
Each single *lagna* consists of five *daṇḍas*;
one *daṇḍa* consists of sixty *pānīyapalas*;
and one *pānīyapala* consists of six breaths (*śvāsa*).
Thus, in one day and night, there are twenty-one thousand six hundred inhalations and exhalations; externally, these are the *daṇḍas* of the sun, while internally they are the breaths.

Thus, regarding "in one day and night," it was likewise stated by the Blessed One in the *Hevajra*: "In the *nirmāṇacakra*, there are sixty-four *daṇḍas*, each consisting of fifty-six and a quarter *pānīyapalas*."
In the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), there are thirty-two *ghatikās* consisting of two *daṇḍas* each;
in the wheel of enjoyment (*saṃbhogacakra*), there are sixteen transitions (*saṃkrānti*) consisting of two *ghatikās* each;
and in the wheel of dharma (*dharmacakra*), there are eight watches (*prahara*) consisting of four *ghatikās* each.
In this regard, the instruction of the Guru is that the sequence for the enjoyment [wheel] is in reverse order within the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*).
Thus, the specific division of time for a day and night is summarized in another minor tantra (*laghutantra*);
however, in the Root Tantra (*mūlatantra*), such as the *Lakṣābhidhāna*, it was taught by the Blessed One in detail.
For example,
in that external world, there is a specific temporal division on each day within the solar year.

Twenty-one thousand six hundred *daṇḍas* are the breaths of the sun; these are the breaths of embodied beings within themselves every day. Thus, there are thirty-six days, each consisting of sixty *daṇḍas*.
Within the internal [body], there are sixty-six breaths per day;
thus, there are twenty-four fortnights consisting of nine hundred and ninety days,
which within the internal [body] consist of nine hundred and ninety breaths.

Likewise, externally, there are twelve months consisting of eighteen hundred and eighteen hundred *daṇḍas*; internally, there are [twelve months] consisting of eighteen hundred and eighteen hundred breaths (*śvāsa*). Thus, externally, the six seasons consist of thirty-six hundred and thirty-six hundred *daṇḍas*.

Inwardly, the four *yugas* consist of 360 breaths each; outwardly, they consist of 540 *daṇḍas* each. Inwardly, the three *kālās* consist of 540 breaths each; outwardly, they consist of 720 *daṇḍas* each.
Internally, they consist of seventy-two hundred times seventy-two hundred breaths;
externally, in each solstice (*ayana*) consisting of ten thousand eight hundred *daṇḍas*, there are two [solstices] internally consisting of ten thousand eight hundred breaths.

Thus, in one day and night, there are twenty-one thousand six hundred *daṇḍas* for the sun externally, which correspond daily to the breaths of embodied beings internally. Here, the inhalation and exhalation of humans constitutes a day and night for the swarms of worms born from their bodies; in that very context, this specific distinction of time is to be understood.

In this world, one month of humans is a day and night for the *pretas*; a year of gods is sixty years for the *dānavas*; and for Śakti, the number of breaths in a cycle (*śvāsacakra*) is a year; and for Bodhisattvas, that very [cycle] is a day and night, and that same day is a single breath of the Lord for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.
Thus, this distinction of time for all [beings] is to be understood on a daily basis, as it was taught by the Tathāgata in various tantras and other scriptures.

Thus, by means of the four seats (*catuḥpīṭha*) and so forth, the wise should understand the specific times, the movement of the yoginīs, and the authority over enjoyment and dissolution within the *Cakrasaṃvara*.
This is the rule for the procedure of worship regarding the specific times, both externally and internally.
Now, the thirty-six family messengers (*kuladūtīkā*) are described.
The thirty-seventh lineage-holder (kulikā) is as follows: in this Root Tantra, Vajravārāhī is the lineage-holder.
The low-born Dombinī is the Ḍākinī; the Śūdrī is Lāmā; the Kṣatriṇī is Khaṇḍarohā;
and the Vaiśyā is [Rūpiṇī].
The embodied Brāhmaṇī,
Kākāsyā, Mlecchī, Ulūkāsyā, and Haddinī.
Śvānāsyā, Mātaṅgī, Śūkarāsyā, Tāpinī, Yamadādhī, and Śavarī.
Yamadūtī is Bhillī,
Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī is Pukkasī,
and Yamamathanī is Barbarī.
Pracaṇḍā, Aṃśukāriṇī,
Caṇḍākṣī, Kalyapālinī, Prabhāvatī, Mālākārī, Mahānāsā, and Hemakārī.
Vīramatī, Kūpakartī, Kharvarī, Veṇunartakī, Laṅkeśvarī, Kaṃsakārī,
Drumacchāyā, Maṇikārī, Airāvatī, and Lohakārī.
Mahābhairavā, Lākṣākārī,
Vāyuvegā, Kośakārī, Surābhakṣī, and Tailinī.
Śyāmādevī is a barberess,
Subhadrā a leather-worker, Hayakarṇā a wood-carver,
and Khagānanā a bamboo-worker.
Cakravegā, Khaṭikinī, Khaṇḍarohā, Kaṇḍukī,
Śauṇḍinī, Śibikā, Cakravarmiṇī, and Naṭī.
Suvīrā is a washerwoman, Mahābalā is a fisherwoman, Cakravartinī is a potterwoman,
and Mahāvīryā is a courtesan.

The Blessed One has stated this rule regarding the ritual for worshipping the *kuladūtīs*: "A mantra-practitioner should worship these, in their respective order, on the external day of enjoyment (*bhoga*) at the time of enjoyment, for the sake of accomplishing worldly siddhis through the expansion of prior karma.
Now, the *samayadūtīs*, who transform into various forms, are described:
here, Vajravārāhī is the *kulikā* (the lineage-holder) who transforms into all forms; Vajradākinī is the dog-faced one (*śvānī*).
Lāmā, Aśvī, Khaṇḍarohā, Hastinī, Rūpiṇī, and Gauḥ.
Pracaṇḍā, Meṣī, Caṇḍākṣī, Aji, Prabhāvatī, Hariṇī,
Mahānāsā, Kharī, Vīramatī, Sūkarī, Kharvarī, and Uṣṭrī.
Laṅkeśvarī, Araṇyaśvānī,
Drumacchāyā, Araṇyasimhinī, Airāvatī, and Gaṇḍī.
Mahābhairavā, Vyāghrī,
Vāyuvegā, Ṛkṣī, Surābhakṣī, and Nakulī.
Śyāmādevī, Camarī, Subhadrā, Jambukī, Hayakarṇā, and Udrī.
Khagānanā, Bidālī, Cakravegā, Kumbhīrī, Khaṇḍarohā, and Kapardikā.
Śaundinī, Karkatī,
Cakravarminī, Matsī, Suvīrā, and Makarī.
Mahābalā, Dardūrī,
Cakravartinī, Kūrmī, Mahāvīryā, and Śaṅkhinī.
Kākāsyā, Godhī, Ulūkāsyā, Mūṣakī, Śvānāsyā, and Śālijātaki.
Śūkarāsyā, Vānari,
Yamadādhī, Gavali, Yamadūtī, and Sallakī.

Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī, Iṣukī, Yamamathani, and Kṛkalāsī—these thirty-six Samaya-deities, who assume the forms of land-dwellers, water-dwellers, and forest-dwellers, shall grant accomplishments to yogins when those yogins know their true nature. Now, those who assume the forms of sky-dwellers are described:
here, Kulikā Vajravārāhī is the transformer of all forms.
Vajradākinī is the blue jay, Lāmā the parrot, Khaṇḍarohā the maina, Rūpiṇī the myna bird, and Kokilā the cuckoo.
Pracaṇḍā, Lābī,
Candākṣī, Pārāvatī, Prabhāvatī, and Bakī.
Mahānāsā, Cataka,
Vīramatī, Cakravākī, Kharvarī, Haṃsī, Laṅkeśvarī, and Pājī.
Drumacchāyā, Vṛkṣāriṇī, Airāvatī, Kākī, Mahābhairavā, and Gṛdhri.
Vāyuvegā, Ghukī, Surābhakṣī, Mṛgāriṇī, Śyāmādevī, and Śikhinī.
Subhadrā, Kukkuṭī, Hayakarṇā, Bhedinī, Khagānanā, Pārī, Cakravegā, and Kruñcā.
Khaṇḍarohā, Kokilākṣī,
Śauṇḍinī, Rajakī, Cakravarmiṇī, and Bhagavatī.
The partridge is possessed of brave sons;
the crane is of great strength; the ruddy goose is a universal sovereign; and the water-crow is likewise.
Mahāvīryā, Balākā, Kākāsyā, Nīlākṣī, Ulūkāsyā, and Cakorī.
Śvānāsyā, Anilā, Śūkarāsyā, Vāgbulikā, Yamadadhi, and Bukki.
Yamadūtī, Tittibhī, Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī, Bheruṇḍī, Yamamathanī, and Ambarakī.
Thus are the thirty-seven yoginīs who transform into the forms of sky-farers.

Having prepared pills from the faultless meats of these land-dwellers, water-dwellers, forest-dwellers, and sky-dwellers—obtained as they may be, together with the five nectars—in the manner to be described, and having consecrated them upon a cremation ground, one should sprinkle the offering substances such as the Vajra of Speech with those [pills]. Then, having purified, awakened, ignited, and transformed them into nectar, the practitioner should offer the obtained sacramental substances (*samayadravya*) to the yoginīs at the time of the wheel-worship. Furthermore, during the time of meditative cultivation, the time of movement, and the time of union, one should place the pill in one’s own mouth, in the mouth of the Wisdom Consort (*prajñā*), and in the mouths of the heroes (*vīra*) and heroines (*vīreśvarī*).
Thus is the rule for the procedure of the pledge-offering (*samayapūjā*).
Now, the locations for the movement of the Yoginīs at the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth, both externally and internally, are described:
externally, on the summit of Mount Sumeru, upon the excellent seat of the universal lotus (*viśvapadmavaraṭaka*).
Within the inner self, at the secret lotus (guhyakamala), the root-seat (mūlapīṭha), Vajravārāhī is the Kulikā;
on the eastern petal of the heart-lotus, at the self-seat (ātmapīṭha), Vajradākinī is located;
on the southern petal of the throat-lotus, at the other-seat (parapīṭha), Lāmā resides.
In the western petal of the navel lotus, at the mantra-pīṭha, is Khaṇḍarohā;
in the northern petal of the forehead lotus, at the tattva-pīṭha, is Rūpiṇī;
and in the pericarp of the crown lotus, at the sarva-pīṭha, Śrī Heruka is to be worshipped in the jñāna-cakra.
Then, in the space of the mind-wheel (*cittacakra*), in the eight directions of Mount Meru: on the eastern spoke at Pūrṇagiri, upon the head, is Pracaṇḍā with Kanda-kapālika;
on the southern spoke at Jālandhara, upon the crest-lock (*śikhā*), is Caṇḍākṣī with Mahākaṅkāla;
on the western spoke at Oḍḍiyāna, above the right ear, is Prabhāvatī with Kaṅkāla.
In Uttāra-arbuda, on the neck, back, and head, are Mahānāsā and Vikatadamstrin; these are the Savīra and Vīreśvarī Bhoginīs in the four pīṭhas, following the clockwise rotation starting from Kuṇḍalā.
Then, in the Īśāna spoke, at Godāvarī, above the left ear, is Vīramatī and Surāvairin;
in the Vāyavya spoke, at Rāmeśvara, between the eyebrows, is Kharvarī and Amitābha.
On the western spoke, at Devīkota, in the two eyes is Laṅkeśvarī-Vajraprabhā;
on the southeastern spoke, at Mālavaka, in the two armpits is Drumacchāyā-Vajradeha.
Thus, in these four secondary seats (upapīṭhas), the Bhoginīs—the Heroes and Heroines—reside in a counter-clockwise rotation starting from Kuṇḍalā.
In this way, one should worship the *pīṭha*, *upapīṭha*, and *bhoginī* *khecarīs* in the mind-wheel (*cittacakra*).
Then, on the circle of the earth, in the eight directions from Meru, one should worship in the speech-wheel (*vākcakra*): in the eastern spoke at Kāmarūpa, in the two armpits, Airāvatī and Aṅkurikā;
in the southern spoke at Oḍra, in the pair of breasts, Mahābhairavā and Vajrajatilā.
Thus, in the two fields, there are the two *bhoginīs*, Savīra and Vīreśvarī;
in the western spoke, Triśakuni; at the navel, Vāyuvegā and Mahāvīra;
in the northern spoke, Kośala; and at the tip of the nose, Surābhakṣī and Vajrahūṃkāra.
Thus, in the two secondary fields (upakṣetra), there are the two goddesses of enjoyment (bhoginī), Savīrā and Vireśvarī.
In this manner, the goddesses of enjoyment of the field and the secondary field [are arranged] by the rightward rotation of Kuṇḍalā.
Then, in the northeast spoke (īśānāra), in Kaliṅga, at the mouth, [is] Śyāmādevī and Subhadra.
In the northwest petal at Lampāka, in the throat, are Subhadrā and Vajraprabha; these are the two Bhoginīs with their Vīras and Vīreśvarīs in the two *chandohas*.
In the southwest petal at Kāñcī, in the heart, are Hayakarṇā and Mahābhairava; in the southeast petal at Himālaya, in the genitals, are Khagānanā and Virūpākṣa;

these are the two Bhoginīs with their Vīras and Vīreśvarīs in the two *upachandohas*. Thus, the Bhoginīs of the *chandohas* and *upachandohas* [are arranged] by the counter-clockwise rotation of Kuṇḍalā.
In this way, the Kṣetras, Upakṣetras, Chandohas, and Upachandohas, along with the Bhoginīs, who are the Bhūcarīs, are to be worshipped by the practitioner in the Vākcakra.

Then, on the surface of the earth within the oceanic circle, in the eight directions from Meru, they are to be worshipped in the Kāyacakras: Cakravegā and Mahābala at the eastern spoke in Pretapurī at the liṅga;
Khaṇḍarohā and Ratnavajra at the southern spoke in Gṛhadevatā at the anus.
Thus, at the two meeting points (*melāpaka*), there are the *bhoginī*s Śaundinī and Hayagrīva in the western spoke in Saurāṣṭra, located in the pair of thighs;
and Cakravarminī and Kāśagarbha in the northern spoke in Suvarṇadvīpa, located in the shanks.
Thus, at the *melāpaka* and *upamelāpaka* [sites], there are the two *bhoginīs*, Suvīrā and Vīreśvarī;

in this way, there are the *bhoginīs* of the *melāpaka* and *upamelāpaka*. Then, by the rightward rotation of the *kuṇḍalā*, in the city on the northeast spoke, [one meditates on] Suvīrā-Heruka on the toes of the feet.
In the northwest spoke, in the ocean, at the two backs of the feet, are Mahābalā and Padmanarteśvara;
in the two cremation grounds, the two serpent-ladies Vīrā and Vīreśvarī;
and in the southwest spoke, in the desert, at the two big toes, are Cakravartinī and Vairocana.

On the eastern spoke at Kulatā, on the two knees, are Mahāvīryā and Vajrasattva; these are the two goddesses of enjoyment (bhoginī) belonging to the cremation grounds (śmaśāna) and the secondary cremation grounds (upaśmaśāna), together with their heroes (vīra) and heroines (vīreśvarī).
Thus, the goddesses of enjoyment of the cremation grounds and secondary cremation grounds are worshipped in the body wheel (kāyacakra) by means of the counter-clockwise rotation of Kuṇḍalā.

In this same manner, the goddesses of enjoyment of the meeting places (melāpaka), the secondary meeting places (upamelāpaka), the cremation grounds, and the secondary cremation grounds are to be worshipped in the body wheel.

By means of the movement of the *yoginīs* in the assembly of the wheels (*cakramelāpaka*) according to the sequence to be described, there is the worship of the movement of the three wheels (*tricakrasaṃcāra*). Then, in the underworld (*pātāla*), in the center of the circles of fire and wind, in the eight directions from Meru, in the great hell of intense smoke and in the eight great cremation grounds (*mahāśmaśāna*):
therein, in the eastern cremation ground, at Śūlabheda, at the gate of the mouth is Kākāsyā.
In the south, at the place of cremation and the right nostril, is Ulūkāsyā;
in the west, at the foul-smelling anus, is Śvānāsyā;
in the north, at the putrid-smelling left nostril, is Śūkarāsyā.
Thus, by the clockwise rotation starting from Kuṇḍalā, [the goddesses are placed as follows]:
Yamamathani in the northeast petal (Īśāna-ara), at the door of the left ear;
Yamadūti in the northwest (Vāyavya) petal, at the door of the right ear.
In the southwest, at the door of the right eye, is Yamadamṣṭriṇī in Ghorayuddha; in the southeast, at the door of the lower lip, is Yamamathanī in Ucchiṣṭa.

Thus, by means of the counter-clockwise rotation of Kuṇḍalā—namely, by clockwise and counter-clockwise rotation in direct and reverse order—the goddesses who enjoy the eight great cremation grounds are to be worshipped in the *cakramelāpaka*.
Thus, in the wheels of gnosis, mind, speech, and body located at the navel, heart, and forehead, as well as in the eight gates beginning with the mouth, there are the gatekeepers;

thus there are thirty-six yoginīs. This is the description of their locations, both externally and internally. Now, the enjoyment, dissolution, authority, and sovereignty of Kulikā and the others are described:
here, for Kulikā, there is enjoyment, dissolution, authority, and sovereignty everywhere, including the Ātmapīṭha and the rest.

Regarding Vajradākinī and the others, according to their sequence, there is enjoyment (*bhoga*) in one's own seat (*ātmapīṭha*), dissolution (*laya*) in another's seat (*parapīṭha*), and authority (*adhikāra*) in the seat of reality (*tattvapīṭha*).
Here, in one's own seat, there is enjoyment; in another's seat, there is dissolution;
and in the seat of reality, there is authority.
In the Mantrapīṭha there is sovereignty;
in another pīṭha there is enjoyment; in the Mantrapīṭha there is dissolution.
In the Ātmapīṭha there is authority; in the Tattvapīṭha, sovereignty;
in the Mantrapīṭha, enjoyment; in the Tattvapīṭha, dissolution; and in the Parapīṭha, authority.

In the *ātmapīṭha* there is sovereignty (*prabhutva*), in the *tattvapīṭha* there is enjoyment (*bhoga*), in the *ātmapīṭha* there is dissolution (*laya*), and in the *mantrapīṭha* there is authority (*adhikāra*); in the *parapīṭha* there is sovereignty.

Thus, according to the division of the four junctions (*catuḥsaṃdhyā*), the movement of the *dūtīs* occurs in the *cakramelāpaka* by way of a clockwise rotation: first in the *jñānacakra* at the navel, and from there, enjoyment in Pūrṇagiri.
Dissolution in Jālandhara, authority in Arbuda, and sovereignty in Oḍḍiyāna.
In Jālandhara there is enjoyment (bhoga), in Oḍḍiyāna dissolution (laya),
and in Pūrṇagiri authority (adhikāra).
In Arbuda there is sovereignty; in Oḍḍiyāna there is enjoyment; in Arbuda there is dissolution.
Jalandhara is the sphere of authority,
Prabhutva at Pūrṇagiri, enjoyment at Arbuda, and dissolution at Pūrṇagiri.

In Oḍḍiyāna there is authority (*adhikāra*), and in Jālandhara there is sovereignty (*prabhutva*). Thus, by the clockwise rotation of Kuṇḍalī, during the rising of Scorpio and its half, the rising of Sagittarius and its half, on the new moon of Mārgaśīrṣa or the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa, or on the new moon of Puṣya or the full moon of Puṣya, the movement of the Yoginīs occurs in the heart at the *cittacakra*. Thence, in Godāvarī there is enjoyment (*bhoga*), and in Rāmeśvara there is dissolution (*laya*).
Sovereignty over Mālava,
lordship over Devīkoṭa, and enjoyment at Rāmeśvara.
Dissolution at Devīkoṭa,
authority over the Godāvarī, and sovereignty in Mālava.
In Devīkoṭa is enjoyment (bhoga), in Mālava is dissolution (laya),
and in Rāmeśvara is authority (adhikāra).
Sovereignty in Godāvarī,
enjoyment in Mālava, and dissolution in Godāvarī.
There is authority at Devīkoṭa and sovereignty at Rāmeśvara;

thus, by the counter-clockwise rotation of the Kundalā, there is the movement of the Yoginīs during the rising of Capricorn in the first half of Capricorn, and during the rising of Aquarius in the first half of Aquarius, within the Heart, which is the Citta-cakra.

Or, externally, regarding the "assembly of wheels" (*cakramelāpaka*), there is the movement of the yoginīs within the mind-wheel (*cittacakra*) throughout the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and secondary seats (*upapīṭha*).
Here, when there is enjoyment (*bhoga*) in Kāmarūpa, there is dissolution (*laya*) in Oḍḍiyāna.
In Kośala there is authority; in Triśakuni, sovereignty;
likewise, enjoyment in Odra and dissolution in Triśakuni; in Kāmarūpa, authority.
Sovereignty over Kośala,
enjoyment in Triśakuni, and dissolution in Kośala.
Authority over Oḍra, sovereignty over Kāmarūpa, enjoyment in Kośala, and dissolution in Kāmarūpa.
The authority is over Triśakuni; sovereignty is over Odra.

These are the fields (*kṣetra*), sub-fields (*upakṣetra*), and places of enjoyment (*bhoginī*). By means of the clockwise rotation of the *kuṇḍalā*, there is the movement of the yoginīs at the Wheel of Speech (*vākcakra*) in the throat, externally at the *melāpaka*.
In Pisces-ascendant and the middle of Pisces, and in Aries-ascendant and the middle of Aries, [there is the sequence] of the Yoginīs.

Thus, when there is enjoyment (*bhoga*) in Kaliṅga, there is dissolution (*laya*) in Lampāka and authority (*adhikāra*) in Himālaya; likewise, in Kāñcī there is sovereignty (*prabhutva*). Similarly, when there is enjoyment in Lampāka, there is dissolution in Kāñcī and authority in Kaliṅga; when there is enjoyment in Kāñcī, there is dissolution in Himālaya.
Sovereignty over Lampāka, lordship over Kaliṅga,
and enjoyment in the Himalayas.
Dissolution in Kaliṅga,
authority in Kāñcī, and sovereignty in Lampāka.

Thus, in the throat, at the Wheel of Speech (*vākcakra*), within the external *cakramelāpaka*, there is the movement of the yoginīs of the fields (*kṣetra*), sub-fields (*upakṣetra*), sacred sites (*chandoha*), and secondary sacred sites (*upachandoha*) by way of the counter-clockwise rotation of Kuṇḍalī. At the rising of Taurus, in the first half of Taurus; and at the rising of Gemini, in the second half of Gemini—there is movement in the throat, at the Wheel of Speech.
Here, when there is enjoyment (*bhoga*) in Pretapurī, then there is dissolution (*laya*) in Gṛhadevatā; there is authority (*adhikāra*) in Suvarṇadvīpa and sovereignty (*prabhutva*) in Saurāṣṭra.
Thus, there is enjoyment in Gṛhadevatā.
Dissolution in Saurāṣṭra, authority in Pretapurī, sovereignty over Suvarṇadvīpa, and enjoyment in Saurāṣṭra.
Dissolution occurs in Suvarṇadvīpa; authority resides in the household deity;
sovereignty in Pretapurī; and enjoyment in Suvarṇadvīpa.
His dissolution is in Pretapūrī;
his authority is over Saurāṣṭra and the household deities.

Regarding "sovereignty": in the *melāpaka* and *upamelāpaka*, the *bhoginīs* [move] by the rightward rotation of the *kuṇḍalā*; in the *kāyacakra* at the forehead, during the rising of Cancer and the first half of Cancer, and during the rising of Leo and the first half of Leo, there is the movement of the *yoginīs* in the external *cakramelāpaka* within the *kāyacakra*.
Here, when there is enjoyment (*bhoga*) in the city (*nagara*), then there is dissolution (*laya*) in Sindh.
In Kulatā there is authority;
in Maru, sovereignty;
and likewise in Sindh, enjoyment.
Dissolution is in Maru,
authority in the city [of Mathurā],
and sovereignty in Kulatā.
In Maru there is enjoyment; in Kulatā, dissolution;
in Sindh, authority; and in the city, sovereignty.
In Kulatā there is enjoyment; in the city, dissolution;
in Maru, authority.

"Sovereignty over the ocean" refers to the movement of the Yoginīs who enjoy the cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*) and secondary cremation grounds (*upaśmaśāna*) by means of the *kuṇḍalā-vāmāvarta* [rotation].

At the rising of Virgo (*kanyā*), during the half of Virgo; at the rising of Libra (*tulā*), during the half of Libra—[this occurs] on the forehead in the body-wheel (*kāyacakra*). In the external wheel-concourse (*cakramelāpaka*), there is the movement of the Yoginīs within the body-wheel. The movement of these twenty-four Yoginīs within the three wheels occurs according to specific times, distinguished by the twelve half-signs (*lagnārdha*) beginning with Scorpio (*vṛścika*).
In this context, when there is enjoyment (*bhoga*) at Śūlabheda, then there is dissolution (*laya*) at Śavadahana;
there is authority (*adhikāra*) at Klinnagandha, and sovereignty (*prabhutva*) at Pūtigandha.
Thus, enjoyment is in the cremation of corpses,
dissolution in the foul odor,
and authority in being impaled on a stake.
In the smell of moisture, there is mastery; in the smell of putrefaction, enjoyment; in the smell of moisture, absorption; in the cremation of a corpse, authority;
in the piercing by a stake, mastery; in the smell of moisture, enjoyment; and in the piercing by a stake, absorption.
They have authority over foul odors and mastery over the cremation of corpses;
thus, they enjoy the great cemetery, as indicated by the clockwise rotation of their earrings.
From midnight, during the first, second, third, and fourth watches, there is a movement through the four gates beginning with the mouth; this also applies to the Yoginīs in the external *gaṇacakra*.
Here, when there is enjoyment (*bhoga*) at the time of a child's death, there is absorption (*laya*) at the bite of a snake, and authority (*adhikāra*) in the remnant (*ucchiṣṭa*).
In a terrible battle, there is sovereignty; likewise, in being bitten by a snake, there is enjoyment;
in a terrible battle, there is dissolution; in child mortality, there is authority; and in leftover food, there is sovereignty.
In a terrible battle there is enjoyment; in being left over, dissolution; in being bitten by a snake, authority;
in the death of a child, sovereignty; in being left over, enjoyment; in the death of a child, dissolution.
